lesson.title: The Electron: Almost Nothing in Mass, Everything in Chemistry
lesson.summary: Electrons are the light, negatively charged particles surrounding the nucleus that govern how atoms bond, react, and form the chemistry of everyday matter.
lesson.body:
If protons and neutrons are the heavy anchors of an atom, electrons are its nimble outer workforce. An electron carries a negative charge equal in magnitude to a proton's positive charge, about 1.602 times 10 to the negative 19 coulombs, but its mass is almost nothing by comparison: about 9.109 times 10 to the negative 31 kilograms, roughly 1/1836th the mass of a single proton. Because electrons are so light, essentially all of an atom's mass comes from its protons and neutrons, while essentially all of its chemical behavior comes from its electrons.

Electrons do not sit inside the nucleus with protons and neutrons. Instead they occupy the space around the nucleus, arranged in energy levels and orbitals that quantum mechanics describes probabilistically rather than as fixed orbits. What matters for chemistry is that electrons, especially the outermost ones called valence electrons, are what atoms use to bond with each other. When atoms share, gain, or lose electrons, they form the covalent and ionic bonds that build every molecule and compound in the world. Protons never move between atoms in ordinary chemistry, and neutrons rarely matter at all for reactivity, but electrons move, shift, and rearrange constantly.

A neutral atom always has a number of electrons equal to its number of protons, because the positive and negative charges must balance for the atom to have no overall charge. This is the direct link between electrons and the proton count already established as atomic number. A neutral sodium atom has 11 protons and therefore 11 electrons. But atoms do not always stay neutral. When a sodium atom loses one electron, it becomes a sodium cation, written Na+, with 11 protons but only 10 electrons, giving it a net charge of positive one. The proton count, and therefore the element identity, has not changed at all, only the electron count has shifted.

A worked example: an oxygen atom has atomic number 8, so a neutral oxygen atom has 8 protons and 8 electrons. When oxygen gains two electrons to form the oxide ion, O2-, it now has 8 protons but 10 electrons, giving a net charge of negative two, from 10 negative charges balanced against only 8 positive charges. This gain of electrons, not any change to the nucleus, is what turns a neutral oxygen atom into a doubly negative ion, and it is exactly this kind of electron transfer that drives ionic compound formation, such as when sodium and oxide ions combine to form compounds.

Electrons were the first subatomic particle discovered, identified by J.J. Thomson in 1897 through experiments with cathode ray tubes, which showed that these negatively charged particles were far lighter than any atom and were present inside atoms of every element. That discovery overturned the older idea that atoms were indivisible and opened the door to understanding atomic structure as a whole, including how proton count, neutron count, and electron count together determine everything from an atom's mass to its willingness to react.
